summary: An index-style memo that lists the RFCs numbered 2900 through 2999 with their titles and basic details. It is a reference aid for finding documents in that range rather than a technical specification. The RFC Editor published a summary like this for each block of one hundred RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a table of contents for one shelf of a huge library, listing every book on the shelf so you can find the one you want.

subtitle: A reference guide to 100 RFCs from 2900 to 2999

tldr.problem: Finding and understanding RFCs can be challenging, especially when multiple related documents are spread across the RFC series.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2999 lists and briefly describes all 100 RFCs numbered 2900 to 2999, providing a snapshot of the standards and informational documents published during a specific period.
tldr.outcome: This summary document makes it easier to discover relevant RFCs in that range and understand their subjects at a glance.

today: RFC 2999 is an Informational document and remains an accurate historical snapshot of RFCs published in the 2900-2999 range as of August 2001. While the individual RFCs it describes have their own current status, this summary itself has not been updated or superseded.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 2999 is a slightly annotated list of all 100 RFCs numbered from 2900 through 2999. It serves as a status report and reference guide for the Internet community. This document does not specify an Internet standard but provides important information about the standards and protocols published during this block of RFC numbers.

The document contains a brief title and description for each RFC in the range, organized as a simple table for easy reference. Some RFCs are marked as being on the standards track, indicating they are either Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or Internet Standards.
sections.plainLanguage: A library card catalog lists all the books in one section so you can find what you need. This RFC does the same for other RFCs.

sections.title: Scope and Coverage
sections.content:
RFC 2999 covers 100 documents: RFCs 2900 through 2999. Each entry includes the RFC number, the principal author or organization, the publication date, and the title. Most entries also include a one or two sentence abstract describing the RFC's purpose.

The summary notes that many RFCs are Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or Internet Standards, which indicates they are undergoing or have completed the standards process. However, the status may change, so readers are directed to the most current Internet Official Protocol Standards document for authoritative status information.
sections.plainLanguage: This lists 100 RFCs, what each one is about, who wrote it, and when it came out.

sections.title: Sample RFCs Covered
sections.content:
The RFCs in this range cover a wide variety of topics. For example, RFC 2960 describes the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), a transport layer protocol. RFC 2945 and 2944 describe the SRP (Secure Remote Password) authentication system. RFC 2988 defines the standard algorithm for computing TCP's retransmission timer.

Other examples include RFCs on network management (MIB definitions), compression algorithms (such as RFC 3051, which uses ITU-T V.44), LDAP directory services, IPv6, DNS extensions, and Internet infrastructure administration.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFCs in this batch cover many different internet technologies: sending data reliably, logging in securely, finding information in directories, and much more.

sections.title: How to Use This Summary
sections.content:
This document serves as a starting point for locating RFCs in the 2900-2999 range. Once you find an RFC number and topic of interest in this summary, you can read the full text of that RFC through the RFC Editor's website or archive.

The summaries are very brief and designed to help identify which RFCs might be relevant to your interests. For detailed technical information, you must consult the full RFC text. Standards-track RFCs are particularly important for protocol implementers and network operators.
sections.plainLanguage: Use this list to find the RFC number you're interested in, then read the full document for all the details.

sections.title: Standards Status and Updates
sections.content:
Not all RFCs in this range have the same status. Some are Internet Standards, which are the official protocols of the Internet. Others are Proposed Standards or Draft Standards, still undergoing the standards process. Many are Informational, meaning they provide useful information but are not protocol standards.

The notation [STANDARDS TRACK] in some entries indicates those RFCs that are part of the formal standards process. Readers seeking information about current protocol standards should consult the Internet Official Protocol Standards document, which is updated regularly and contains authoritative status information for all RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Some RFCs are official standards that everyone must follow. Others are proposals being tested, or just useful information for programmers.
